title: Dream Creatively
author: John
summary: Watching transient artists and van-dwellers camped outside his beach bungalow, the author is reminded of a sailing dream he and his wife Judy chose not to pursue forty years ago, and uses it to work through when a man should chase a personal dream versus build a shared one with his family. He argues that most people default to what they already know they can do because it feels safe, and that dreaming honestly requires setting aside the practical 'how' until you've answered the more basic question of whether something is truly wanted. The essay's turning point is his wife's refusal to spend their savings on a boat instead of a house — a decision he now credits with the stable, adventure-filled life they built together — and he closes with a reflection exercise for readers to distinguish 'my dream' from 'our dream' before committing to either.
points: Bob Proctor's three-category framework for goals — what you know you can do, what you think you can do with effort, and what you really want — explains why most people settle for the safest option.
The essay's central move: a delayed dream isn't necessarily an abandoned one, since the author is still dreaming about sailing to Mexico decades after choosing to buy a house instead.
The practical discipline he recommends is separating the question of desire from the question of feasibility: ask 'is this something I truly want?' before asking 'can I afford it or do I know how?'

His marriage lesson is explicit: 'a lasting marriage' depends on learning the difference between the life you personally want and the life you and your spouse are building together, and holding both without abandoning either.
quotes: What all of these travelers had in common was a dream and they put that dream into action. They were making it happen while most of us sat at home complaining about the various restrictions we were facing because of the pandemic.

Don’t let practicality kill a dream before you’ve even given yourself permission to consider it. For a little while, set aside the question of how. Don’t immediately ask whether you can afford it or whether you know exactly how to get there.

Choosing one dream doesn’t mean you have given up all the others forever. A delayed dream isn’t necessarily an abandoned dream. Sometimes a dream is delayed because something more important needs to happen first.
One of the great lessons of a lasting marriage is learning the difference between the life you want and the life the two of you are building together.
